title: Elizabeth Barrett Elopes with Robert Browning
text:
In the 1840s Elizabeth Barrett was one of the most famous poets in England, and also an invalid who rarely left her room at 50 Wimpole Street in London. Her father, Edward Moulton-Barrett, a wealthy and domineering man, did not allow any of his children to marry.

In January 1845 the younger poet Robert Browning wrote to her: "I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett," adding that he loved her too. She answered, and a correspondence began that grew into nearly six hundred letters. In May 1845 he visited her for the first time, and after that came regularly, always when her father was out. They fell in love and knew that he would never consent.

On 12 September 1846 Elizabeth, forty, slipped out of the house with her maid and married Robert at St Marylebone Church. She returned home as if nothing had happened. A week later she left for good, taking her maid and her dog, Flush, and the couple traveled to Italy.

Her father disinherited her and never spoke to her again. He returned her letters unopened. In Italy, her health improved remarkably. In 1849, at forty-three, she gave birth to a son. The couple settled in Florence. In 1850 she published Sonnets from the Portuguese, the love poems she had written to Robert during their courtship, and other works followed. She died in his arms in 1861.
lesson: A parent's control can drive a child to choose love over family, at a lasting cost to both. Love that is forbidden instead of understood is love lost.
people: Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Robert Browning, Edward Moulton-Barrett
source: The Letters of Robert Browning and Elizabeth Barrett Barrett, 1845 to 1846 (1899); Margaret Forster, Elizabeth Barrett Browning (1988)
